name: Design a Tamper-Evident Audit Log
intent: Record who did what and when across every service, keep it for years, and make any edit, deletion or quiet rewrite of the record detectable, even by the people who run the system.
codeTitle: a hash-chained log with Merkle checkpoints
finalIntro: One privileged action being recorded, sealed, and later checked.
prompt: Design the audit log for a platform used by regulated customers. Hundreds of services record security-relevant events: sign-ins, permission changes, reads of sensitive records, deletions and exports. Auditors and investigators must be able to trust the record, even against an insider with database access. Entries must be kept for seven years, held longer when a lawsuit demands it, searched in seconds and exported on request, and the log itself must be protected from the people who read it.
functional: Capture who did what, to which object, when, from where, and with what outcome
Store entries so they cannot be changed or deleted in place
Prove that the log has not been altered, and show where if it has
Search by actor, object, action and time, and export a range for an auditor
Keep entries for the retention period, delete them afterwards, and hold specific ones longer on a legal hold
Control who can read the log, and record that access too
nonFunctional: Never silently lose an event, even when a service or the log is down
Absorb 200,000 events per second at the peak without slowing the services that emit them
An event is searchable within about 10 seconds
Any alteration or removal of sealed history is detected, including by an administrator with write access to the storage
Verifying a single entry takes a few hashes, not a scan of the whole log
Seven-year retention at a sensible cost, with old data moved to cheap storage

firstAttempt.text: Every service writes a row to an audit table in the main application database: time, user, action, object. Anyone with database access can query it. Old rows are deleted by a nightly job after seven years.
limits: An administrator, or an attacker who got in as one, can update or delete rows and nobody can tell
Audit writes share the database and the transaction budget with the application, so heavy auditing slows the product and an outage of one takes the other down
Events are only as good as what each team remembers to record, in whatever shape they chose
Searching years of rows with free-text filters scans a huge table and competes with live traffic
Nothing protects the table from the people who read it, and nothing records who looked, or lets a legal hold stop the nightly delete

steps.title: Make the log append-only, and chain every entry to the last
steps.problem: A table that an administrator can update or delete from proves nothing, because a changed row looks exactly like an unchanged one.
steps.fix: Put one collector in front of a separate log store, and give the services no direct access to it. The collector stamps each event with who (an authenticated actor and the service acting for them), what (action and object), when (a time from a trusted clock, plus a sequence number), where from and the outcome. It then appends the entry to the log, and each entry stores the hash of the previous entry together with its own content. Changing or removing any entry changes every hash after it, so a verifier walking the chain finds the first break. The store itself only accepts appends.
steps.tradeoff: Edits and deletions in the middle become visible, and the format is the same for every service. A chain alone cannot see someone who rewrites the whole tail with recomputed hashes, or who cuts off the newest entries, and it forces entries into one order per chain.

steps.title: Absorb the peak with a queue and several chains
steps.problem: Hundreds of thousands of events per second cannot go through one writer that must append to a single chain in strict order, and services must not stall when the log is slow.
steps.fix: Services hand events to a local agent that writes to a durable ingest queue, with the event id as an idempotency key. Consumers append from the queue into many partitions, each with its own hash chain, chosen by a hash of the actor or tenant so that one actor's events keep their order. If the log is down, the queue and the local agent buffer on disk and replay later. The services get a fast acknowledgement, and overload is shed from the lowest-value events first, never from security events.
steps.tradeoff: Throughput scales by adding partitions, and an outage of the log no longer loses events or blocks the product. There is no single global order any more, only an order per partition plus timestamps, and the log lags the real action by a short time.

steps.title: Seal history with signed Merkle checkpoints held elsewhere
steps.problem: Someone who can write to the store can edit an entry and recompute every later hash, producing a chain that verifies perfectly, or can drop the newest entries.
steps.fix: At a regular interval, each partition is sealed: a signer computes a Merkle root over the entries of the block, signs it together with the partition's head hash and length, and publishes the signed checkpoint to a system the log operators cannot rewrite, such as an external transparency service, a separate account with write-once storage, or a public ledger. To verify, recompute the chain and compare it to the checkpoints. To prove one entry exists, hand over the entry and its path of about sixteen sibling hashes up to the signed root, which an auditor checks without reading the rest of the log.
steps.tradeoff: Rewrites and truncations of sealed history are caught, and single-entry proofs are tiny. Entries newer than the last checkpoint are protected only by the chain, so the interval is the window an insider could use, and the signing key must be guarded with great care.

steps.title: Tier storage into write-once archives, with retention and legal holds
steps.problem: Seven years of events is hundreds of terabytes, which is too much to keep on fast disks, and deleting on schedule is wrong when a lawsuit says the data must be kept.
steps.fix: Sealed blocks move to a write-once archive in object storage, compressed and partitioned by tenant and day, with object locks so that no one can delete them before the retention date, not even an administrator. A legal hold is a record in its own table that names a tenant, an object or a time range; the expiry job checks it before every deletion and skips anything held, and placing or lifting a hold is itself an audited, two-person action. Expiry removes whole blocks, and the checkpoints still verify the remaining chain because each block's boundary hash is kept.
steps.tradeoff: Storage becomes cheap and deletion becomes a controlled, provable process. Archives are slower to query, a hold can quietly grow the bill for years if nobody reviews it, and personal data inside entries may conflict with erasure rights, so entries should hold identifiers rather than the content.

steps.title: Index recent history for search, and export ranges with proofs
steps.problem: Investigators need answers in seconds, such as every export by this user last month, and scanning archives for each question is far too slow.
steps.fix: A separate consumer reads the sealed log and builds a search index on actor, object, action, tenant and time, keeping recent months in fast storage and older ones in cheaper tiers. The index is a derived copy and can be rebuilt from the log at any time. A search returns entries together with their position (partition and sequence), so any hit can be checked against the log. An export is an asynchronous job that writes a signed file for a range, with the checkpoints and Merkle proofs an auditor needs to verify it offline.
steps.tradeoff: Queries are fast and never touch the source of truth, and exports are self-verifying. The index lags the log by a few seconds, costs storage in addition to the log, and must never be trusted as proof: only the chain and checkpoints are.

steps.title: Protect the log from its readers, and audit the auditors
steps.problem: The log holds a map of everything sensitive that happens, and the people with the most access to it are the ones it is meant to watch.
steps.fix: Reading goes through an access gate with single sign-on and multi-factor authentication, role-based and tenant-scoped permissions, and a narrow purpose for each role, so a support engineer sees their tenant and an auditor sees only an approved range. Write access is limited to the collector's identity; operators of the storage cannot sign checkpoints, and the signer cannot read the data. Every search, view and export on the log is itself written to the log as a new entry, and the keys that sign and encrypt it are rotated and kept in a vault. Alerts fire on bulk exports, on a failed verification and on unusual access, and alterations to the log's own configuration need two people.
steps.tradeoff: No single person can both change history and hide it, and the access trail is as trustworthy as the rest. Strict separation slows incident response, adds roles to maintain, and the log of log-reads grows quickly, so it needs its own retention rules.

failures.scenario: The log store is unreachable for twenty minutes
failures.impact: Services keep acting, and without care their events would be dropped, leaving a hole exactly when something odd may have happened.
failures.answer: The agent next to each service and the ingest queue buffer events durably and replay them when the store returns, with event ids making the replay safe. If a buffer fills, the service fails closed for the most sensitive actions, such as changing permissions, rather than acting unrecorded, and other events are sampled or dropped by priority with a counted gap that is itself logged.

failures.scenario: An administrator rewrites the tail of a partition and recomputes the hashes
failures.impact: The chain verifies perfectly, so a walk through the log alone finds nothing wrong.
failures.answer: The recomputed head and Merkle root no longer match the signed checkpoint published outside the operators' control, so verification fails at the first sealed block that was touched. Entries newer than the last checkpoint are the exposure, which is why the interval is short and checkpoints are cross-checked by a second party.

failures.impact: An attacker could forge history and sign it, and every earlier checkpoint is in doubt.
failures.answer: Keys are held in a hardware module and rotated on a schedule, with each checkpoint naming the key that signed it. Because checkpoints are also anchored outside the system with a timestamp, a forgery signed later cannot predate the leak, so history before the incident stays provable. After a leak the key is revoked, a new chain epoch begins, and the gap is documented.

failures.scenario: A lawsuit arrives while the expiry job is deleting year-seven data
failures.impact: Deleting entries that are under a legal hold is a legal problem of its own, and keeping everything forever is a cost and privacy problem.
failures.answer: The expiry job checks the hold table for every block before deleting and skips any block that overlaps a hold, with the check and the skip both logged. Placing a hold takes effect immediately and blocks are locked in the archive, and lifting a hold needs a second approver and starts the normal expiry clock again.

failures.scenario: The search index is lost or silently falls behind
failures.impact: Investigators get empty or incomplete results and may conclude that nothing happened.
failures.answer: The index is derived, so it is rebuilt by replaying the sealed log, and each result page states how far the index has caught up to each partition. A periodic job compares the index's counts and Merkle roots with the checkpoints, and a search that spans an unindexed range says so and falls back to scanning the archive.

alternatives.title: How to make history tamper-evident

options.name: Database permissions and triggers only
options.con: Anyone with enough privilege removes the protection, and nothing proves it did not happen

options.name: Hash chain per partition
options.pro: Cheap, detects edits and deletions in the middle
options.con: A full rewrite of the tail with new hashes is invisible without something outside the chain

options.name: Hash chain plus signed Merkle checkpoints anchored elsewhere
options.pro: Detects rewrites and truncation, and gives short proofs for one entry
options.con: Needs a signer, an external anchor, and a decision about the checkpoint interval

options.name: A public blockchain or ledger service
options.con: Slow and costly per write, so it is used only to anchor the checkpoint roots, not each event

alternatives.pick: Chain per partition with signed Merkle checkpoints, anchored to an external system.

alternatives.title: Where entries live

options.name: Application database
options.con: Shares load and permissions with the thing being audited

options.name: Dedicated append-only store with object-locked archive
options.pro: Independent permissions, cheap retention, deletes blocked by the platform

options.name: A managed immutable ledger database
options.pro: Hash chaining and proofs built in
options.con: Vendor-specific, with limited search and throughput for the top volumes

alternatives.pick: A dedicated append-only store with an object-locked archive, plus a derived search index.

alternatives.title: Chain granularity

options.name: One global chain
options.pro: A single total order, simple to explain
options.con: One writer, so it cannot reach hundreds of thousands of events per second

options.name: A chain per partition or tenant
options.pro: Scales out, and a tenant can verify only their own history
options.con: No global order, only per-chain order plus time

alternatives.pick: A chain per partition, keyed by tenant, with global ordering recovered from timestamps when needed.

alternatives.title: What to do when the log cannot be written

options.name: Fail open and carry on
options.con: Actions happen unrecorded, which is the thing the log exists to prevent

options.name: Fail closed for everything
options.con: An audit outage becomes a full outage

options.name: Buffer, and fail closed only for the most sensitive actions
options.pro: Most work continues and the riskiest actions stay recorded
options.con: Needs a classification of actions and well-sized buffers

alternatives.pick: Buffer durably, fail closed for high-risk actions, and log every counted gap.
